analysis.one_liner: Bans toxic chemicals like PFAS and BPA from food packaging.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a House floor vote; it died in the Energy and Commerce Committee at the end of the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal food safety law to declare five groups of chemicals unsafe to use in anything that touches food: ortho-phthalates, PFAS ('forever chemicals'), bisphenols including BPA, styrene, and antimony trioxide. These chemicals are common in food packaging and can migrate into food, and research links them to health harms, especially for children and pregnant women. The ban would take effect two years after enactment, and regulators would have to weigh effects on vulnerable populations when considering substitutes.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who eats packaged food, since the chemicals listed can leach from packaging into food. The strongest protections would be for infants, children, pregnant women, the elderly, and workers and communities with disproportionate exposure, groups the bill specifically requires regulators to consider.

how_it_helps.text: The bill legally deems ortho-phthalates, PFAS, bisphenols (BPA, BPS, BF, BAF and related compounds), styrene, and antimony trioxide unsafe for use as food contact substances, removing them from food packaging [S2].
It takes effect two years after enactment, giving manufacturers time to switch packaging materials [S2].
When regulators evaluate replacement chemicals, they must consider harms to vulnerable populations including infants, children, pregnant women, the elderly, and workers [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers that make phthalates, PFAS, bisphenols, and styrene, and food and packaging companies that would have to reformulate products within two years. Some compliance costs could be passed through to consumers in slightly higher prices.

drawbacks.text: The ban is written by chemical class, not by individual chemical: the PFAS definition covers any man-made substance with at least one fully fluorinated carbon atom, so it sweeps in many chemistries at once rather than banning only those proven harmful in food contact [S2].
A two-year deadline for reformulating packaging imposes real compliance costs on food and packaging manufacturers, which could be passed to consumers as higher prices.

Some of the listed chemicals have long been permitted under existing FDA food-contact rules, so the bill overrides the agency's current safety determinations with a flat legislative ban rather than case-by-case review.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Reducing phthalate, PFAS, and bisphenol exposure through food packaging addresses a real and widespread health concern, and the two-year lead time softens the transition for industry. The main honest objection is the breadth of class-wide bans, which could eliminate some packaging uses before safer substitutes are fully proven; on balance the health benefits outweigh the compliance costs, though the bill is a blunt instrument.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on October 26, 2023, with eight original Democratic cosponsors [S1][S4].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced [S4].
On November 3, 2023, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress [S4].
The bill ended the 118th Congress without a committee vote or a floor vote, so it did not become law [S1][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chemical manufacturers and food packaging companies are better off, since they face no ban on phthalates, PFAS, bisphenols, styrene, or antimony trioxide in food contact materials. Consumers continue to be exposed to these chemicals through packaging.

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban listed toxic chemicals from food packaging.

for.name: Reps. DeLauro, Dingell, Norton, Pingree, Velazquez, Watson Coleman, Lynch, and Grijalva
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction; the bill drew 13 cosponsors in total, all Democrats.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair Cathy McMorris Rodgers, R-WA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no action on it; no hearing, markup, or vote was scheduled before the Congress ended.

against.name: Subcommittee on Health, House Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on November 3, 2023 and took no further action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the Republican-controlled committee never acted on the bill.

industries.industry: Chemical manufacturers (phthalates, PFAS, bisphenols, styrene, antimony compounds)
industries.note: The bill would eliminate their food-packaging market for these chemicals by deeming them unsafe under federal food law. Their continued legal use keeps exposure pathways open for consumers.
They would bear reformulation costs within two years to remove the banned substances from packaging. Continuing to use them means the chemicals can migrate into the food they package.

Companies selling safer substitute packaging would gain customers as the banned chemicals come off the market, and the bill directs regulators to assess substitutes with vulnerable populations in mind.
